topic.title: We fight the fees we can see
topic.claim: We spend ten minutes angry about a ₹15 platform fee and sign a loan with a ₹5,000 processing fee without reading the page.
topic.moment: You uninstall a food app over a new fee and then tick 'I agree' on a personal loan in thirty seconds.

turn.actually: We're careful about fees that show up on a screen we look at every day.

topic.feeling: Embarrassed, because I know exactly which fee I ignored.
topic.villain: Pricing that puts big costs in fine print and small costs on the checkout screen
topic.because: A small fee we see every day feels like an insult. A big fee we see once, in small type, doesn't feel like anything.
topic.payoff: The fee you complain about is rarely the fee that costs you the most.
topic.behaviour: People rage about delivery and convenience fees but accept loan, insurance and card charges unread.
topic.mechanism: We react to what we can see often, not to what costs the most.
topic.group: Young earners with their first loans and cards
topic.send_to: The friend who switched apps over ₹10 and has never read their loan agreement.
topic.why_now: App fees are now a regular thing to be angry about, while loan fees still pass without notice.

score.why: We rage at a visible ₹15 fee and sign a loan's big fee unread; a problem the reader didn't know they had, and it stings.

topic.title: Moving back costs the second offer
topic.claim: Moving back to a tier-2 city saves you rent but quietly costs you something nobody counts: your next job offer.
topic.moment: You work remotely from your hometown, life is cheaper, and the recruiter calls stop.

turn.believed: Moving back is just a cost-of-living win.
turn.actually: Big cities pay you for the options you have, not just the job you hold.

topic.feeling: Happier at home, and slowly afraid I've fallen off the map.
topic.villain: Job markets packed into a few metros
topic.because: Your salary rises when another company wants you. Fewer companies around you means fewer reasons for anyone to pay you more.
topic.payoff: Before you move, count how many companies within an hour of you would hire you tomorrow. That's what you're giving up.
topic.behaviour: Professionals move home for remote roles and see their salary growth slow down.
topic.mechanism: Pay grows with competing offers, and offers live in metros.
topic.group: Remote and hybrid professionals weighing a move home
topic.send_to: The friend who keeps saying 'I'll just work from home in my city'.
topic.why_now: Remote roles are shrinking while metro rents keep rising, and a lot of people are doing this maths right now.

score.why: Going home looks like a cost win, but you give up the job options that push your salary up; mixed feelings, a real turn.

topic.title: The hamper is a sales cost
topic.claim: The Diwali hamper that lands at your desk from a vendor isn't gratitude; it's next year's deal, gift-wrapped.
topic.moment: A dry-fruit box with a vendor's logo arrives the week before Diwali, addressed to whoever signs the purchase order.

turn.actually: They're a sales budget line, sent to whoever decides the next contract.

topic.feeling: Flattered, then aware I'm being worked on.
topic.villain: Business-to-business sales that run on relationships
topic.because: In deals between companies, the person who decides is worth more than the price. A hamper is a cheap reminder of who remembered them.
topic.payoff: Notice who in your office gets the biggest box. That's who really decides what gets bought.
topic.behaviour: Vendors send festive gifts mostly to procurement and decision-makers.
topic.mechanism: Goodwill with the person who signs is cheaper than winning on price.
topic.group: Office workers in mid-size and large companies
topic.send_to: The colleague whose desk turned into a dry-fruit shop this Diwali.
topic.why_now: Diwali hampers have just done their rounds, so everyone has a fresh example.

score.why: The vendor's Diwali hamper is next year's deal in gift wrap; funny, a desk everyone has seen, and a hidden motive.

topic.title: The phone shop sells you the EMI, not the phone
topic.claim: When phone prices jump, the real gatekeeper is not the price tag but the loan approval at the counter.
topic.behaviour: Buyers walk in with a budget, get pointed to an EMI scheme, and leave with a cheaper brand, a refurbished phone or nothing. Total sales value stays flat while fewer phones leave the shop.
topic.mechanism: When components cost more, sellers keep the sales value up by raising prices, and the shopper's real filter becomes credit. Tighter loan checks decide who goes home with a phone.
topic.group: Young salaried buyers upgrading a phone on instalments
topic.moment: You pick the phone, the shopkeeper says 'EMI ho jayegi', and then the approval does not come through.

turn.believed: A phone is expensive, so you save up and buy it.
turn.actually: Most phones are bought on credit, so whether the lender says yes matters as much as the price.

topic.feeling: behind, as if you are being judged at the counter
topic.villain: A retail model that depends on instalment credit and tight underwriting
topic.because: Rising memory costs push prices up and shops lean on loans to close sales. When lenders tighten, the shop loses the buyer and the buyer loses the phone.

proof.fact: Offline phone volumes fell 18-20% from Dhanteras (6 Nov) to the day after Diwali, while sales value stayed broadly flat because prices rose.
Retailers said only 60-70% of logged loan applications were approved.

topic.payoff: Ask the shop for the full price instead of the monthly number. That is the phone you can actually afford.
topic.send_to: The friend who has changed phones twice on EMI and never knew the total
real_details: Value-conscious buyers moved to HMD, Lava, Ai+, Tecno and itel, or to pre-owned and refurbished phones
topic.news_peg: AIMRA said retail smartphone volumes fell 18-20% across Diwali week, reported 2026-11-11
topic.why_now: Post-Diwali phone numbers show who could not complete a purchase.

score.why: At the phone counter, the EMI approval decides what you can buy as much as the price does; the feeling of being judged at the counter, with one sourced figure.
